title: Isaiah’s Vision and Scriptural Witnesses
english: … holy, Lord Sabaoth; heaven and all the earth are full of his glory” (Isaiah 6:3).

And after other things he says: “He said to me: Say to the people: Hearing you will hear and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown thick, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them” (Isaiah 6:9-10). And in between, among other things, he adds: “And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord Sabaoth. And one of the seraphim was sent to me” (Isaiah 6:5-6), and what follows.

Now this Isaiah knows that the Lord Sabaoth and King who was seen is God the Father himself. But Paul, in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, declared that it is the Holy Spirit, speaking out in these words: “The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, saying: Go to this people and say to it: Hearing you will hear and will not understand” (Acts 28:25-26), and the rest, as set out above.

And John in his Gospel determined that it is the Son of God. For he said: “Though Jesus had done so many signs, they could not believe, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them” (John 12:37-40). And at once he adds: “These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory” (John 12:41), that is, the glory of the Son of God. So much, then, more or less, on these matters.

But hear also other texts of the same force. David, in the ninety-fifth Psalm, sang on the lyre in the person of God the Father in these words: “Your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with this generation and said: They always go astray in their heart; and they did not know my ways. So I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest” (Psalm 95:9-11).

Paul, writing to the Hebrews from the same psalm, determines that it comes from the Holy Spirit, in this way: “As the Holy Spirit says,” he writes, “Today, if you hear my voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation, on the day of testing, where your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years” (Hebrews 3:7-9). And Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles, putting the Jews to shame from the same scripture, said: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).
Likewise Moses, for his part, says that it was the Lord who led the Hebrews out of Egypt. In Deuteronomy he says: “For the Lord alone led them, and …” (Deuteronomy 32:12)

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u06): retranslated from the Greek. The old draft garbled 19.9 ('Paul … finding the Holy Spirit to be, declared thus, interjecting', reader report), reversed Isaiah 6:6 ('he was sent to one of the seraphim'), made Isaiah 6:3 a full sentence though the section opens mid-quotation, mistranslated 19.13 ('the same threatening scripture') and Deuteronomy 32:12 ('was alone with them'), and gave a stray reference (Isaiah 6:5) to Didymus' own comment in 19.8. References: abbreviated names written in full; Acts 28:25 widened to 28:25-26; Psalm 95:7-11 narrowed to 95:9-11 (Didymus quotes LXX Psalm 94:9-11); Hebrews 3:7-8 widened to 3:7-9. Ends mid-sentence as the Greek does.
